parent.name: Sicilian Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 1.e4 with ...c5 to trade a flank pawn for White's d-pawn, which leaves Black a central pawn majority and a half-open c-file in return for White's lead in development and space. This asymmetry is the point: Black plays for a win rather than equality. The usual pattern is White attacking on the kingside while Black counterattacks on the queenside along the c-file (...b5, ...Rc8), often with opposite-side castling in the sharpest lines. The root is a crossroads: after 2.Nf3 (about 80% of master games, s1) it branches into Najdorf, Dragon, Scheveningen, Classical, Sveshnikov, Taimanov and Kan, which range from forcing and theory-heavy (Najdorf, Dragon, Sveshnikov) to flexible and solid (Kan, Classical, Taimanov). White's anti-Sicilians (Alapin, Closed, Grand Prix, 2.d3) avoid the Open Sicilian and are quieter. The root as a whole is the most played and most analysed opening at club and master level (s1).

parent.name: Sicilian Defense: French Variation
parent.moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 e6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6
parent.overview: 2...e6 is a gateway rather than a set-up: after 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Black chooses the Taimanov (...Nc6), the Kan (...a6) or the Scheveningen (...d6, ...Nf6), with 3.Nc3 giving the Paulsen/Kan/Taimanov move orders. Black opens the diagonal for the f8-bishop and prepares ...d5 or ...Nc6/...a6 in a flexible way, with a solid ...e6/...d6 pawn chain and queenside counterplay. The name 'French' is only a naming convention: the pawn structure is Sicilian, not a French one. White's main choice is 3.d4 (about 61% of moves at 2500); rarer third moves are 3.d3, 3.g3, 3.c3 and Westerinen's 3.b3 (Bb2, occasional in the 1970s). At higher levels play is heavily theoretical.

parent.name: Four Knights Game
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Nc3 Nf6
parent.overview: Both sides develop both knights, so the root position is a symmetrical, classical tabiya from which White chooses the character of the game. The main branches are 4.Bb5 (the Spanish Four Knights), 4.d4 (the Scotch Four Knights), 4.g3 (the Glek System) and 4.Be2/4.Bc4 quieter alternatives. After 4.Bb5 Black can mirror with 4...Bb4 (the Double Spanish, highly symmetrical and drawish) or go for the Rubinstein 4...Nd4 for imbalance; 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4 Bb4 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.Bd3 d5 leads to an open, more active game in which White usually keeps the initiative. The opening has a drawish reputation and often gives quiet positional play, although sharp variations (Belgrade Gambit, Halloween Gambit) exist. It was almost forgotten after the 1930s and enjoyed a renaissance in the 1990s; Short, Adams and Shirov have played it, and it is popular at club level because it needs little theory.

parent.name: Center Game Accepted
parent.overview: The root is the crossroads after 2.d4 exd4, with Black a pawn up and White to move. White's main choice is 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qe3 (Paulsen Attack): the pawn is regained, Black gains a tempo on the queen, and White castles queenside after Nc3 and Bd2, using the queen on e3 and the d-file to aim at g7 and the kingside. Black has calm, sound ways to equalise (4...Nf6, 4...Be7 preparing ...d5, 4...g6, 4...Bb4+) and can counterattack White's king on the queenside. The alternative 3.c3 is the Danish Gambit, where White gives one or two pawns for open lines and development. 3.Nf3 or 3.Bc4 lead to Scotch, Scotch Gambit, Petroff-type or Urusov positions. Overall it is old and rarely played at the top level, though with a modern revival (Shabalov, then Nepomniachtchi and Erigaisi, Shirov, Adams) as a practical, objectively equal surprise.

root.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. d4 exd4 3. Qxd4 Nc6

parent.name: Center Game
parent.overview: White strikes the centre at once: 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 regains the pawn and opens the game, at the cost of an early queen that Black hits with 3...Nc6. The queen goes to e3 (Paulsen's Attack, 4.Qe3), and White develops quickly with Nc3, Bd2, Bc4 or Be2, castles queenside and aims the queen and the semi-open d-file at g7 and the kingside, or pushes the h-pawn. Black has calm, sound set-ups (4...Nf6, 4...Be7 preparing ...d5, 4...g6, 4...Bb4+) and equalises with accurate play. Opposite-side castling can turn it into a race. Instead of 3.Qxd4, White can play 3.c3 (Danish Gambit), which is a separate gambit branch.

parent.name: Italian Game
parent.overview: White develops the bishop to c4 aiming at f7 and prepares to take the centre with c3 and d4 or, more quietly, d3 (s1, s2). The root is a crossroads: 3...Bc5 (Giuoco Piano) mirrors White's set-up, 3...Nf6 (Two Knights) invites sharper play, and 3...Be7 (Hungarian) is passive and solid (own understanding for the last). Today's main practical line is the Giuoco Pianissimo with c3, d3 and slow manoeuvring, which became fashionable in the 1980s-2000s and again in the 21st century as a way to avoid the Berlin (s1). The older 4.c3 and d4 lines and the Evans Gambit are sharper (s1). It is fundamentally sound with modest winning chances (s1). It is described as accessible to beginners yet used by Giri, So and Vachier-Lagrave (s3).

parent.name: King's Indian Defense: Normal Variation
parent.moves: 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 g6 3. Nc3 Bg7 4. e4 d6
parent.overview: This root is the King's Indian reached by the move order 1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.c4 (the same position as 3.Nf3 in the 2.c4 move order). It is not a distinct opening: it is the ordinary King's Indian, where Black fianchettoes with ...Bg7, castles, and strikes at White's centre with ...e5, ...c5 or ...f5. White's choice of set-up decides the character: the classical 4.Nc3 and e4 leads to the locked-centre opposite-wing race (c4-c5 against ...f5-f4), while the Fianchetto Variation (g3, Bg2, O-O, Nc3) is quieter, positional, and has less forcing theory. The data subtree groups 4.e4 Normal Variation lines (the majority of games) under this root, so it mixes both. Black's success depends on timing and coordination rather than automatic aggression.

parent.name: Caro-Kann Defense
parent.overview: Black plays ...c6 to support ...d5 and so challenges the e4 pawn with a sound pawn structure, while keeping the light-squared bishop free to come out to f5 or g4 before ...e6 (the French Defence's main drawback, at the cost of a tempo). Black accepts less space early and tends to get a resilient, hard-to-break structure with few weaknesses and good endgame prospects. Play is mostly positional and manoeuvring; it is called more solid and less dynamic than the Sicilian (s1). The Advance (3.e5 Bf5) and Panov-Botvinnik (3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4) lines are more combative, and the Advance became the most popular White try in the 21st century. Main branches: Classical (4...Bf5), Advance, Exchange, Panov, 4...Nf6 lines, Gurgenidze (...g6), Two Knights (2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3) and Fantasy (3.f3). This is a crossroads root after 1...c6; the pawn structures differ by branch.

parent.name: Slav Defense
parent.overview: Black supports d5 with ...c6 so that the centre is held by pawns while the light-squared bishop stays free to come out (usually to f5 or g4) before ...e6. The root is a crossroads: after 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 Black chooses the Pure Slav with ...dxc4 (active bishop, ...e5/...c5 breaks), the Semi-Slav with ...e6 (c6-d5-e6 triangle, theory-heavy and often sharp: Meran, Botvinnik, Anti-Meran), or the Chebanenko ...a6. White can also play the Exchange (cxd5 cxd5), a symmetrical structure with queenside minority attack ideas that has a drawish reputation, or quiet systems with 3.e3 or 3.Bf4. The Slav is played by many world champions (Botvinnik, Smyslov, Anand, Kramnik) and is regarded as sound; sources treat it as solid with room for counterplay rather than a forced-draw defence.
